text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNRead clock rates from the metric, derive an effective potential from conserved quantities, and distinguish the horizon, photon sphere, and ISCO. Connect to foundations: An entry to general relativity: light, clocks, and gravity ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Start from a spacetime ruler A metric specifies how spacetime intervals are measured. Take the Schwarzschild vacuum metric as the supplied solution, then derive consequences using conserved quantities and algebra. The full tensor calculation solving the field equations is outside this lesson. ds²=−A(r)c²dt²+A(r)−1dr²+r²(dθ²+sin²θ dφ²) A(r)=1−2rgr, rg≡GMc², R≡rrg Here r is the areal radius: spheres have area 4πr². It need not equal radial proper distance. Coordinate time t is normalized to a distant static clock. Our gravitational radius is rg = GM/c²; the Schwarzschild radius is twice this value. This is an exterior vacuum solution. A star needs a different interior solution. The exterior can also describe a nonrotating spherical star, but interpret the horizon sketch below as a black-hole exterior. 02Static clocks and light received far away For a clock at fixed spatial coordinates, ds² = −c²dτ². Substitute zero spatial increments into the metric to obtain its proper time τ relative to t. A local clock continues to run normally for an observer beside it. dτdt=√(1−2/R), 1+z=νemν∞=1√(1−2/R) The redshift formula assumes a static emitter and a static receiver at infinity. Moving emitters require additional kinematic effects. Remaining static outside the horizon requires support; a stationary clock cannot be placed on the horizon itself. The panel keeps R strictly greater than two. 03Reduce radial motion using conserved quantities Consider a massive test particle moving freely in the equatorial plane. Time-translation and rotational symmetries supply the following conserved quantities. Neglect the particle’s self-gravity and radiative backreaction. These orbit constants are separate from the mass parameter defining the spacetime. ℰ=A(r)dtdτ, ℓ=r²dφdτ, λ≡ℓcrg, j≡λ² Divide the metric by dτ², set ds²/dτ² = −c², and substitute the constants. Rearranging isolates the radial kinetic term. This is an exact test-particle relation in the supplied metric, rather than an expansion in weak gravity. −c²=−c²ℰ²A+1A(drdτ)²+ℓ²r² 1c²(drdτ)²+U(R)=ℰ² U(R)=(1−2R)(1+jR²)=1−2R+jR²−2jR³ Radial motion requires ℰ² ≥ U. The additional −2j/R³ term changes the inner barrier. U is dimensionless and is compared with squared energy ℰ², not with ℰ. A potential plot alone is not an integration of a chosen trajectory. 04Find circular orbits and test stability For a circular orbit, radial velocity and the potential slope vanish. Differentiate at fixed j and clear denominators. The resulting quadratic exposes both circular branches and the parameter at which they merge. dUdR=2R²−2jR³+6jR⁴=0 R²−jR+3j=0, R±=j ± √(j²−12j)2 j=R²R−3 (R>3) A minimum gives radial stability; a maximum gives instability. Evaluate the second derivative while keeping angular momentum fixed, and then insert the circular-orbit relation. Do not differentiate along a family that changes j. d²UdR²circular=2(R−6)R³(R−3) R>6: stable, 3<R<6: unstable RISCO=6, jISCO=12, ℰISCO=√89 At R = 6 the radial restoring term vanishes: this is the marginal endpoint of the stable circular branch. ISCO does not forbid matter at smaller radii. Infall and accelerated fluid motion are different from stable circular test-particle geodesics. 05The photon sphere and horizon are different radii For light, use ds² = 0. The rest-mass term disappears and the normalized radial potential is W below. Differentiate it to locate the circular null orbit. Its maximum makes that orbit unstable. W(R)=1−2/RR², dWdR=−2R³+6R⁴=0 ⇒ Rph=3 The horizon is at R = 2, the photon sphere at R = 3, and the ISCO at R = 6. They are not three material surfaces. Also distinguish the photon orbit’s areal radius from the impact parameter for capture measured at infinity. Sketch of areal-radius ratios; neither a proper-distance diagram nor an image of the distant shadow. bcrit=rph√A(rph)=3√3 rg Schwarzschild-coordinate coefficients become singular at the horizon, whereas suitable coordinates describe infall across it. This differs from the curvature singularity at r = 0. The panel remains outside and does not draw horizon-crossing trajectories. 06Run clocks and compare circular branches Clock playback advances distant time and computes the proper time of a supported clock at fixed radius. Changing angular momentum compares potential curves; it does not animate a test-particle orbit. The two operations answer different questions. Try j = 16 to compare an unstable circular orbit at R = 4 with a stable one at R = 12. At j = 12 they merge at R = 6; below that value no massive circular geodesic exists. Use the displayed branch labels to connect the graph to the algebra. The solution library compares this exact vacuum solution with fluid equilibria and similarity models. Kerr and Tomimatsu–Sato entries are listed with their lesson availability explicitly distinguished. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. Double the mass. How do physical horizon, photon-sphere, and ISCO radii change, and what happens to a static clock rate at fixed r/(GM/c²)? Show the answer and reasoning All three physical radii double because they scale with GM/c². At fixed dimensionless R, the clock factor √(1−2/R) is unchanged; the time unit GM/c³ doubles. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide. References may use different notation or normalization. Panel methods and approximations are stated in the text.
